a: People perceive colors differently when looking at the same object due to a combination of biological, neurological, and psychological factors. The most well-known cause is color vision deficiency, commonly called color blindness, which affects approximately 8% of men and 0.5% of women of Northern European descent. This is caused by a genetic mutation that affects the cone cells in the retina — humans typically have three types of cones sensitive to red, green, and blue light, but those with color vision deficiency may have cones that are less sensitive or entirely missing for certain wavelengths. Beyond color blindness, even people with normal color vision perceive colors differently due to variations in the exact sensitivity of their cone cells, which is influenced by genetics. The brain's interpretation of color signals also varies — the visual cortex processes and integrates color information differently in each person. Age-related changes, such as the yellowing of the lens, can shift color perception toward the blue end of the spectrum. Cultural and linguistic factors also play a role — different languages categorize colors differently, and studies have shown that speakers of languages with more color terms are better at distinguishing between similar shades. Lighting conditions, eye fatigue, and individual differences in attention and memory can all affect how colors are perceived. Additionally, some people experience synesthesia, where colors are associated with non-visual stimuli like sounds or emotions, further diversifying color perception. These individual differences mean that what one person sees as 'red' may appear slightly different to another, even though both people use the same word to describe it.
